case_info.scenario: A 53-year-old man received a diagnosis of stage IV melanoma with metastatic disease to the spine and brain 3 months before presentation. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node). Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]). The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure). One week later, he received encorafenib, aBRAFinhibitor.1Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.

case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

case_info.answer: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

case_info.answer: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. case_info.answer: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

case_info.caption: Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.
